reviewBoundary: Four complete new junior insertion texts paired as two practices. Diary and guide source structures retained, including candidate counts and quoted/heading gaps. Same-author cohesion and all-alternative review only, not independent calibration.

units.title: Two diaries: a visitor and a riverside ride
units.alignmentNote: Pairs two complete four-gap/five-candidate diaries, each with a use-once rule and one unused sentence, following the recorded task structure.

materials.title: A visitor at lunch
materials.text:
Tuesday, 14 May

Today a student from our partner school spent the morning with our class. At lunch, I showed her the canteen menu. She could read some English, but several dish names were unfamiliar. ____1____ Then we walked along the counter together.

She pointed to a dish and asked whether it contained eggs. I was about to guess from its appearance. ____2____ So I asked the member of staff instead. He checked the ingredients and gave her a clear answer.

We chose our food and found two seats. I worried that I would have to keep talking throughout lunch. In fact, my visitor asked me about the clubs on a poster behind us. ____3____ Soon I was explaining our film club and asking what activities she enjoyed at home.

After lunch, she thanked me for helping. I had expected to need impressive facts about our school. What mattered more was taking time with ordinary questions. ____4____ Tomorrow I will show her where the club meets, and she has promised to bring a photograph of her own school.
candidates: A. Her question gave our conversation a natural beginning.
B. I explained the words I knew without choosing for her.
C. A friendly visit could grow from those small exchanges.
D. But the colour of the food could not tell me everything in it.
E. I decided she should eat nothing and leave immediately.
materials.instruction: Read the whole diary. Use each option at most once; one sentence is not needed.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: B responds to unfamiliar dish names while preserving the visitor’s choice. A refers to a later question, C reflects at the end and D cautions about ingredients. E contradicts the lunch they enjoy.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: D checks the unsafe impulse to infer ingredients from appearance and leads to asking staff. A is the club question, B menu language and C final reflection. E abandons the visit rather than checking.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: A refers to the visitor asking about the poster and prepares the club conversation. B belongs at the menu, C concludes and D concerns ingredients. E contradicts the continuing friendly lunch.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: C sums up ordinary questions leading to friendship and the next meeting. A is the earlier starting question, B menu help and D ingredients. E is incompatible with the planned next-day visit.

materials.title: A different route to the river
materials.text:
Sunday, 22 June

This morning my aunt and I cycled to the riverside café. We usually take the main road, but part of it was closed for repairs. Before leaving, we checked a map. ____1____ It was longer, but it used quieter streets.

At the first turn, I wanted to keep going straight. My aunt asked us to stop somewhere safe and look again. ____2____ The river was on the other side of that line, so we needed the road leading to the bridge.

We reached the café later than usual. I apologised for my mistake, but my aunt was not annoyed. We had allowed extra time and had no appointment to miss. ____3____ We sat outside and watched boats pass while we waited for our drinks.

On the way home, I recognised several corners without looking at the map. Still, we checked before the bridge because two streets looked similar. ____4____ Knowing when to stop and confirm the route had been more useful than pretending I could remember every turn.
candidates: A. The pause gave us a chance to enjoy the place without rushing.
B. We chose an alternative route through a nearby village.
C. I had learned part of the route, not every detail of it.
D. We threw the map away before leaving the house.
E. I had confused the railway line with the river on the map.
materials.instruction: Read the whole diary. Use each option at most once; one sentence is not needed.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: B explains the new route and gives longer one in the following sentence a referent. A is café time, C later reflection and E a particular map error. D contradicts consulting the map on the journey.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: E names the mistaken line, explaining the river on the other side and the bridge correction. A concerns the café, B initial planning and C final learning. D makes the ongoing map check impossible.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: A develops having no urgent appointment into an unhurried café stop. B is departure, C conclusion and E the earlier error. D contradicts their careful use of the map.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: C balances recognition with checking similar streets, preparing the lesson about confirming details. A, B and E concern other stages. D conflicts with the repeated useful map checks.

units.title: Two guides: recipes and plant care
units.alignmentNote: Pairs two complete five-gap/seven-option guides. Three printed headings, quoted gap2 and missing-heading gap5 retained; no extra use-once instruction is imposed.

materials.title: Sharing a family recipe
materials.text:
Sharing a family recipe can be a pleasant way to learn about one another. Before asking for one, explain what the class plans to do with it. A recipe for a private display is different from one that will be published online. ____1____ Nobody should discover afterwards that a personal contribution has travelled further than expected.

Make participation a choice

Not everyone wants to describe food from home. Begin your invitation with, "____2____" A student can still help arrange the display without giving a family recipe.

Explain unfamiliar measures

A small cup or spoon may mean something very specific in one kitchen. ____3____ Giving a volume or showing the actual container makes the instructions more useful to someone cooking elsewhere.

Keep personal details private

An interesting recipe does not need a home address or a child's full family history. ____4____ Ask before including even a short personal note, rather than assuming that everything shared in class belongs on the display.

____5____

Before the display opens, let each contributor read the final version. A missing ingredient or changed number can make a real difference. The student should also be able to remove a personal detail that no longer feels comfortable to share.
candidates: A. Check the finished version together
B. Tell contributors where their work will be seen.
C. Take part only if you feel happy to do so.
D. Do not assume that every reader owns the same size.
E. Include only the information needed for the agreed purpose.
F. Every family must provide a recipe, even if they object.
G. A final copy can never contain a mistake.
materials.instruction: Read the complete guide and choose the best option for each gap. Two options are not needed. Keep the printed headings and quotation marks.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: B states audience and publication scope, preventing the surprise described next. A is final checking, C voluntary invitation, D measures and E privacy. F forces contribution and G ignores errors.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: C is a quoted invitation making participation optional, supported by another role being available. A is a heading, B scope, D measures and E information limits. F contradicts choice; G is irrelevant to permission.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: D explains why a home-specific cup needs volume or an example. A, B, C and E concern checking, audience, choice and privacy. F and G are unsupported absolute demands.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: E limits details to the agreed purpose and prepares asking before personal notes. A is the final heading, B scope, C choice and D measurement. F compels disclosure and G denies possible mistakes.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 5.
questions.explanation: A heads the final paragraph on contributor review and corrections. B, C, D and E are sentences for other gaps. F and G oppose the guide’s voluntary, checked publication.

materials.title: Looking after a borrowed plant
materials.text:
A neighbour may ask you to care for a plant while away. Saying yes is easier when you know what the task involves. Some plants need more frequent attention than others. ____1____ A clear request helps you decide whether you can actually provide the care.

Ask for a demonstration

Watching once can be easier than remembering a long explanation. You might say, "____2____" Notice how the owner checks whether water is needed, not only how much is poured.

Keep the place suitable

The windowsill may already have been chosen for its light and temperature. ____3____ If the plant must be moved temporarily, ask where else it can safely stand.

Report a problem early

A change in the plant's appearance may have several possible causes. ____4____ Describe what you see and ask for advice rather than adding extra water every time something looks wrong.

____5____

Before the owner leaves, agree on how to get in touch. Check whether someone else can help if you become unavailable. This is particularly useful when a short absence unexpectedly becomes longer, and the plant needs care beyond the original dates.
candidates: A. Tell the owner promptly if a leaf or stem changes unexpectedly.
B. Could you show me what you normally do?
C. Set up a way to communicate
D. Watering every hour is suitable for every plant.
E. Find out the dates and the kind of attention required.
F. Do not move it simply to make the room look tidier.
G. A written contact number makes all further care unnecessary.
materials.instruction: Read the complete guide and choose the best option for each gap. Two options are not needed. Keep the printed headings and quotation marks.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 1.
questions.explanation: E requests timing and tasks, developed by the clear request and decision about capacity. A is problem reports, B demonstration, C final heading and F position. D and G make false universal guarantees.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 2.
questions.explanation: B is a quoted request for the demonstration named in the heading, leading to observing the owner’s check. A reports trouble, C is a heading, E planning and F position. D replaces observation with an unsupported schedule; G dismisses care.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 3.
questions.explanation: F preserves the chosen light and temperature unless a move is necessary. A, B, C and E concern other stages. D ignores different needs and G incorrectly replaces care with a number.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 4.
questions.explanation: A gives an early report of observed change and leads to asking advice without guessing a cause. B demonstrates routine, C communication heading, E dates and F position. D prescribes excessive universal watering and G denies ongoing care.

questions.prompt: Choose the best option for gap 5.
questions.explanation: C is the heading for contact methods, backup helpers and changed dates. A, B, E and F are sentences for earlier gaps. D and G contradict responsive care.
